I am glad the hon.
gentleman has drawn my attention to that. I have a profound faith in the genius of the people of Canada to govern themselves; I have profound faith in the optimism of the Canadian people; and I have a profound faith in the judgment of the people of Canada, and I believe that arguments directed to local prejudices and race passions do not appeal to our people. Examine the pages of our political history, and you will find that when the people of Canada tire of a government they do not turn it out piecemeal, but they wake up one fine morning and completely annihilate it.
They will soon annihilate this Government.

This Government will go down to defeat in time, but not so long as hon. gentlemen opposite are divided on the trade policy, as they are to-day. The usual course is for the people of Canada to put a government in power with a large majority, and to let that government govern the country, but as soon as the government does not legislate to suit them, they turn that government out of power in good shape, as happened in 1911. The moment the late Liberal Government attacked the traditional trade policy of the country, that very moment the people said, we want none of you, and out you go. In the great province of Ontario, the central province of Canada, where manufacturing has been carried to its highest state of development, there is where the Conservative party got their chief support. The result of the last elections, taking them generally, show that where you have diversity of employment and established industries, the people believe in protection. British Columbia, which has coal deposits, fisheries, horticultural lands, farm lands, diversified climate, diversified employment for the people, did not want reciprocity, and the seven members who represent that province are to-day supporters of the right hon. the Prime Minister. In Manitoba, where manufacturing is developed to a certain extent, but not to the same extent as in the eastern provinces, the Conservative party made gains also. In Saskatchewan and Alberta, in one case there was no change, and in another case there was a loss of two seats. Why was this? The people of these provinces are interested in only one industry, and, having no diversified employment, they require a large number of working people at certain times of the year, but have no employment for them at other times. The people of these two provinces, it is said, want free trade. But, Mr. Speaker, if I judge the people of Canada aright, on the whole they are decidedly opposed to free trade, and it is for us to find where the trouble is with these provinces, and if there is a remedy to apply it. I believe, Sir, that if there were manufacturing communities scattered throughout Alberta and Saskatchewan, you would no longer hear from the people of those provinces any talk about free trade. You will find that these people will be protectionists, the same as the people in eastern Canada. Why are these people not . protectionists to-day? For the lack of two things: they have not cheap power and they 
have not cheap transportation. But these are some of the things to which this Government might well address itself. I will attempt to show the House how this problem may be solved, in my judgment. There are great water-powers in Canada, and one of the causes that will yet make Canada industrially great is to be found in the splendid water-powers scattered throughout the length and breadth of this country. Within a few miles off the city of Winnipeg theire is a waterfall capable of developing
500,000	horse-power. Now, one horse-power to five people is about what they require for an industrial city. lSo, in that waterpower on the Winnipeg river alone we have the means to keep going am' industrial city of 2,500,000. Now, the public domain in these western provinces belongs to this Government-coal lands, water-powers and everything else. I say to this Government: Address yourself to that question; find out ' where the water-powers are; develop them and sell power, cheap power, to Manitoba and the other provinces. My hon. friend from Calgary (Mr. Bennett) knows that about 50,000 horse-power awaits development on the rivers within fifty miles of that city. At five people to each horse-power, this would furnish power for a city of 250,000 people.
It so happens that nature in dealing with Canada has been prodigal with her gifts, she seems to have placed things just where we require them. I have shown that at Winnipeg and Calgary we have these water-powers. There are other sections where water-powers do not exist and cannot be developed. But there we have another natural resource w'hich can be converted into energy-I refer to the great beds of lignite coal underlying the soil of these prairie provinces. Any one who has paid attention to mechanics during the past few years will have observed that the gas producer for low-grade coal is a fact. It produces what is known as producer gas at a low rate of expense. The lignite coals of the West are such as can be successfully used to create that gas, and that gas will not only produce power, but it can be made the means of beating homes and factories.
It is not very good for lighting, though it can be used for that purpose. So, I say to this Government:	Continue the examination you are making into the lignite fields of the West; find out where the industrial centres are or are to be; find out how to

develop the power of lignite coal and sell it at a cheap rate thus encouraging the people to go into manufacturing. If you do this, you will have no more worry about free trade. In advocating this, I am simply pointing to the same course which has been followed in the East, for the East grew by developing its natural resources. I received in this morning's mail a booklet from Nova Scotia. The foreword is as follows:
The position to-day of the manufacturing
industries of Nova Scotia is shown in this nic-ture-story. This country with its half million inhabitants affords a typical example of modern industrial growth.
That is the example I am attempting to picture for our prairie provinces of the West, with their great hidden natural resources.
At one time exclusively a farming and fishing region, the province now possesses 1,480 manufacturing establishments, paying out $11,000,000 yearly to 38,000 employees. The industrial ascendency of Nova Scotia is broad based upon its immense deposits of coal, its great forests, its farms, its fisheries, its water-powers.
That can be duplicated in the West, and if we pay proper attention to these great natural resources it will be duplicated in the West. Besides the power which can be generated from lignite coal, there is a byproduct in the form of nitrogen, which can be combined with sulphuric acid to make ammonia sulphate, which is most useful as a fertilizer and for which there is an endless demand.
These are some of the things which the West can do. As an example of what can be accomplished, I need not go farther than this province, in which we can point out what has been done in the development of water-powers. Consider what has been accomplished at Niagara. Did you see, Mr. Speaker, the vast delegation that came here the other day to ask this Government to subsidize radial electric railways in Ontario? Could such a thing have been thought of before Niagara had been developed? Not at all. Niagara power has made possible for this province this and many other things, and if its water-powers are developed, the same thing will come to pass in the West.	,
As I say, the policy of our friends opposite tends directly to free trade, and my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier)-for whom, let me say, I have profound respect; he has carved high his nitch in our temple of
fame-can hardly deny that his policy tends directly to free trade. We have in biology a condition known as ' reversion to type.' A man may inherit the qualities possessed by a progenitor of several generations back, which qualities, after being latent for a time, may develop strongly. Atavism this condition is called; and the distinguished gentleman who leads the Opposition is a case of political atavism- he is reverting to type.
I have some material on the cost of living, but this I will not submit, because I do not wish to occupy too much time.
I wish to say a word about the progress made since my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) came to this country. I congratulate him on the number of converts he has made, judging by the speeches made in this House. He frequently refers-and I give him great credit for being an expert dialectician-to the economic progress of England and the doctrine of free trade. Mr. Speaker, the doctrine of free trade apparently suits the people of England-though we must not be too sure of that. But to hear the hon. gentleman you would think that England had always been a free trade country. England had a greater protection system than Canada ever had, and she had it for 500 years instead of for thirty or forty years, as Canada has had it. When we reach the same stage of economic development as they had reached in England, we may have free trade, too. In England they did not adopt free trade until they had developed an artisan to compete successfully with the best artisans in the world. Let me point out that England in former times had a double protection, not only the protection of import duties, but the protection of her trade guilds as well; and if ever there was a protectionist institution it was the trades guilds of England. They were close corporations. England in time developed this great industrial machine, and not until then did she adopt free trade. And she adopted that policy at a most fortunate time, before the great industrial nations, Germany and the United States, became what they are to-day. She adopted it at a time when practically the whole world was at war, and we know what war does for a country; it paralyses commerce and industry and destroys everything except the fighting spirit of the people. Following the adoption of free trade in England, came the war between Germany and Austria, paralysing the industrial energies of those two countries.

Does he not see that he is digging a pit for his own feet when he says that; as he must see that things which he condemns in unmeasured terms are approved of by the Government which he is supporting?

Almost like 'adequate.'

Now, I desire to say a few words with regard to the implements tariff reduction. Generally, while tariff reductions are an important thing to us in the West, yet, in comparison with the removal of restrictions on our trade, they are of little importance. We have often been told in this House, and were told again by my hon. friend from South Perth (Mr. Steele) that between 1878 and 1896 the Conservative Government made tremendous

reductions in the tariff duties. How did they succeed in reducing these duties? Why, first they laised them and then they took them down-. If they wished to get credit for reduction on that basis, I wonder that they did not put the duties up to one hundred per cent before knocking them down to twenty. Surely it would look better to say that the duties had been reduced by eighty per' cent than to say that they had been reduced by fifteen per cent. But what did the friends of hon. gentlemen opposite do when they were in power during the period referred to? I think I am right in saying that they found the duties on agricultural implements generally at seventeen and one-half per cent and they put them up to thirty-five per cent, and left them there during nearly all the time they were in office. There may be some particular items of which that is not true, but speaking generally it covers the facts. You must remember also that the late Government made an effort to reduce these duties, some by two and one-half per cent and some by five per cent, but through the operations of the big interests and the efforts of those who support the present Government the changes were not made. If the duties were not reduced it was not through the fault of that Government but through the fault of their opponents.	*
We hear something of the reductions proposed in this Budget, and comparisons are made with the object of making us believe that these reductions are far more important than those that would have been made under the reciprocity arrangement. The present reductions refer to three items only-harvesters,- reapers and mowers. The reciprocity arrangement covered, I think, seventeen or eighteen items, and the reduction on all these excepting four was five per cent, the same as is proposed under this Budget, and a very few other items 2J per cent. We were told at that time 'l.at the 178i
reductions under reciprocity were insignificant and were of no use to the people. But now even less reductions are said to be very important. I find that for the year ending March 31, 1911, we imported harvesters, the most important item effected by the present arrangement, to the value of $215,129. But of ploughs we imported six or seven times as much- $1,371,234. But the duty on ploughs is not affected by the reductions proposed under this Budget, while there was to be a reduction of 5 per cent under the reciprocity arrangement. The same is true of threshing separators, of which we imported $2,176,077 worth-more than ten times as-much as we imported of binders. In the face of these facts, I do not see how any one can claim that the reductions now made are to be compared with those which would have been made under reciprocity. We were told that the reductions under reciprocity were valueless, that they were so insignificant as not to be worth considering. If that be true, how much more valueless are the present reductions? 1 do not admit that they are valueless; I think we should be prepared thankfully to receive small mercies from the present Government, because I am sure that that is the only kind of mercies we will ever receive from them. We are thankful for the little things that they have done for us, but we would be more thankful if they would do something worth while. While I say that we are thankful for these things; while I say that we would be glad to have a further reduction of the duty on agricultural implements and other articles, I want to be distinctly understood as saying that nothing of that kind can be accepted for a moment as a substitute for that to which we are entitled-a free market for our produce; an opportunity freely to market, without restrictions, our wheat, our barley, our flax, our oats and other produce wherever the people of any other country are prepared to receive them.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the Finance Minister on the presentation he has made to the House of the condition of the finances of Canada for the past year. Notwithstanding the settled gloom and evidences of despair apparently existing in the minds of hon. gentlemen opposite; notwithstanding the depression that they claim exists from one end of Canada to the other, the Minister of Finance has been able to report a surplus.

i
The last speaker (Mr. Levi Thompson), or the one who proceeded him on the other side (Mr. Nesbitt), admitted that there had been surpluses during the last three years aggregating over $93,000,000, and this was the only complaint he had to make with regard to the financial condition of our country. I can imagine what a wail would have gone up from our friends on the other side had there been a deficit-but we are glad to know that there has been a surplus. In view of a legacy the like of which few governments have had handed down to them-a legacy of years of reckless and wanton extravagance-I think we are to be congratulated on the financial condition in which we now find ourselves. As a result of this legacy which has been handed down by hon. gentlemen opposite, we are confronted with a problem such as has, I believe, never confronted the people of this country before; one that will give the Government serious concern, but one which, I have no doubt, they will be able to adjust satisfactorily.
I have been- very much impressed with the tone of the debate so far. Almost without an exception the members from western Canada get up in their places in this House and discuss the questions before the people of this country to-day from the standpoint of their province alone, practically ignoring the other portions of Canada. I am sorry that we have not sufficiently advanced in this country to feel that we are a united people with a common object in view; with an ideal before us that we are all striving to realize and work out in the very best interests of the people as a whole. Naturally, we must give and take; we must make sacrifices for the interests of the country at times, but in the end I have no doubt that they will redound to the benefit of the whole country. As I have said, I regret the tone displayed by quite a number of hon. gentlemen opposite in discussing these questions before the House. The same attitude characterized the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, who even went so far as to say that the people of western Canada will grow grain for eastern Canada and for other countries of the world as well. Apparently the whole aim and object of the hon. members from western Canada is to grow grain to feed the people of Europe. They utterly forget that the people of Canada have to be fed; they utterly forget that we have a market here in Canada that is being supplied by the very people with whom hon. gentlemen

have been clamouring to enter into closer relationship. The best market in the world is our home market; let us never lose sight of that fact. We have permitted the people of New Zealand to send us butter-yes, we have permitted the people of Ireland to ship potatoes here to feed the people of Canada. In the United States they are growing mutton which is being consumed by the people of Canada; they are raising horses which are being used on Canadian farms. Yet we placidly get up and say:	Let us grow wheat;
wheat is the aim and object of our existence; if we only had free markets, see what we would do. And then there comes the wail: but we cannot grow wheat at the prices that we are getting at the present time. I was somewhat surprised this afternoon to hear the hon. member for the north riding of the county which I represent (Mr. Nesbitt) say: we in North Oxford grow wheat for the straw; we do not grow it for the grain at all. Wheat is not such a very important commodity after all; it is the straw we grow it for in Oxford. Let me tell the hon. gentleman that in 9 p.m. Oxford we grow the finest wheat that is grown anywhere; we grow from 35 to 40 bushels to the acre and we are getting $1.01 a bushel for it at the present time. Hon. gentlemen say:	Remove the tariff on our
wheat and in Ontario we will get our wheat from Kansas. That is exactly what we will do, but in Ontario we do not want Kansas wheat; we want our own wheat and we want more than that; we want the byproducts of our wheat to remain in this country. I want to say to the hon. gentlemen who are so anxious to grow wheat that growing wheat is not the only requirement of a successful agriculturist. Growing wheat is not the basis of agriculture in this country; if you follow the history of agriculture in all European countries you will find that it was when the people departed from grain growing as a specialty and went into mixed farming and stock-raising that they began to realize greater profits. Oh, our western friends say; you must not say anything about that to us; you people in eastern Canada do not know anything about conditions in the West. I think it was the hon. member for PTovencher (Mr. Molloy) who, in discussing this matter some time ago upon the motion for free wheat, said: you people down in eastern Canada may go into mixed farming, but we do not propose to be tied up to any business which requires attention from January to January and

which necessitates your getting up early in the morning and sitting up late at night. We want something easier than that, and we are going to grow wheat. With our friends from the West it is wheat, wheat, every day of the year. I have heard this wail from people who have been in western Canada only a few years. They have gone there and, finding the land ready for the plough, they have mined the fertility that has been stored up there for centuries, without any regard to the result which that course :s going to bring about.
Let me tell the hen. gentleman that that system is bound to bring poverty to this country. But, as the member for West Kent (Mr. McCoig) said: If you do not let these western farmers get their wheat into the United States, they will go into mixed farming, and what will happen? They will be raising hogs and cattle; they will be coming down here by thousands and tens of thousands, and they will overrun the province of Ontario with these products. If they come, we will have great game anyway, if we do not have anything else; but I do not anticipate any trouble in that respect. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle complains that he cannot get his wheat into the United States. He can get his wheat into the United States to-day without paying any duty on it whatever. He does not need to worry about that. But let him get busy like other farmers in Canada and pay close attention to his business; let him show that he is a proper farmer and not a miner of the soil, and then he will find that he has not' such difficulties to contend with. What do you find? Sir, you find, notwithstanding their weary wail about what we would have had under reciprocity-
I would ask my hon. friend if he has ever been out in the West, and if he has seen my farm ? Will he undertake to say that he farms better than I do ?

I am not talking
about your farm; I am talking about your arguments, and I am telling you you can get your wheat into the United States and get more money for it if you want to without paying any duty. You can feed your wheat and send your stock over there and you do not have to pay any duty on it. They talk about wider markets in the United States, and all that sort of thing. You have to-day, under the present United States tariff, all the advantages that you would have had under reciprocity and you have not any of the disadvantages, yet they
ignore all these things. No, it is wheat, wheat, wheat, nothing else but wheat. Let me say that we in Ontario grow considerable wheat, and we do not grow it simply for the straw either. But we find there are other branches of farming that pay much better than growing wheat, and for that .reason we do not grow anything like the wheat we used to. But I will admit that the virgin soil of western Canada is rich and fertile.
I was rather struck with the remarks of Professor Robertson before the agricultural committee here last session, or two years ago, pointing out what the Conservation Commission had observed with regard to the farms of whose production they were keeping a record, that in the old settled districts of Manitoba there was an actual decrease from year to year in the production of the farms. This is only what you would naturally expect, and if by any means the price of wheat should drop so low that the people in western Canada cannot make it pay I have not any doubt that the genius of those people, because I know a great many of them, will find a way out of the difficulty. You have in western Canada, I will admit, as fine a class of people as you will find anywhere. You have the youth and the brawn, and many of them from the province of Ontario, and I know their object and aim in many cases their plan to get cheap lands of the West and they hope by growing wheat for a few years, by the increase in value of the land they can realize sufficient profit to dispose of their land at a profit and move out of the country again. That is an unfortunate state of affairs. I believe that after they have been there for a number of years they will change their ideas. Western Canada is not a country for people to desert. There are many things about western Canada which appeal to every one, and I would be the last one that would put a straw in the way of our friends in western Canada that would be considered as detrimental to their interests.
On the mattter of free wheat the member for Qu'Appelle stated that the Americans shipped bran into this country. I have here a clipping from the Toronto Globe of January last which says that the price of bran is $2 to $3 per ton mure in the United States than in Canada, and that is correct. In my own county, notwithstanding the wheat straw that we grow up there, we import thousands of tons of bran and shorts every year that are fed there in order to increase our dairy produce. I

suppose ours is one of the largest importing counties in Ontario of these commodities and they tell us. we cannot mill in Canada, that the United States mills are the proper places to mill our wheat. I say that what the people of the United States can do Canadians can do if you will only give them time to do it. It would be, I consider, a calamity if we were now to lose our mill feed and all these things that go to build up the agricultural industry of the country. We are handicapped, I will admit, in not being able to grow corn as easily as they do in the United States, with the exception of a few counties in western Ontario. The county represented by the member for West Kent (Mr. McCoig) can grow as fine corn as can be grown anywhere but we have had illustrations of our ability to raise the finest kind of stock. Western Canada has demonstrated it. You have had stock in Chicago in competition with stock from all over the world and have demonstrated that the grains grown in western Canada are sufficient to produce the finest beef that can be grown in the world. I have not the slightest doubt that in a few years all these things will be remedied.
I cannot understand how the hon, the junior member for .Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) in his speech claimed that we could not compete with the millers even in' Great Britain, in the manufacture of flour. With the splendid water powers that we have here, with the cheap facilities for grinding I cannot understand how it is possible that we cannot do that. But I believe that one of the reasons why that is claimed to be the case is on account of ocean rates which discriminate against us. If the grievances of hon. gentlemen were the ocean rates they would have something more reasonable than what they are complaining about to-day.
I was also a little surprised the day the Budget speech was delivered by the Minister of Finance to find that the Toronto Globe came out on the first page with statements to that effect and the further announcement that he was to be followed by the junior member for Halifax, who was going to move an amendment that wheat and agricultural implements should be put on the free list. I was somewhat surprised when no amendment wa3 forthcoming and still more surprised when that gentleman, instead of going on with his reply to the Minister of Finance, asked leave to adjourn the debate until after the Easter holidays. 
However he was granted the privilege of adjourning the debate for that day. I do not know what conferences have been held by hon. gentlemen opposite or what they are going to do. If I did not know them so wiell, I believe I would almost come to the conclusion that they did not intend to move any amendment at all; but now I suppose, in order to save their faces, they will move some kind of an amendment even if it is only their policy just for the moment. We all remember the negotiations that took place at Washington between two members of the late Government and representatives of the United States Government. Our friends were invited down there, and no doubt were as generously entertained as our neighbours to the south knew how to do. Afterwards, during the campaign of 1911, we quoted statements that had been made by prominent men in the United States during the general election. We were told that those statements were not correct at all. I may say now that I am, and have been, surprised that hon. gentlemen opposite consider that they have not received their dues even after the people have expressed their views on the reciprocity question in the contest-no, I will not say the contest, but in the election of 1911. We have been told that so far as Ontario is concerned the issue was not reciprocity at all, and that passion and prejudice influenced the people there. During my experience covering a number of years, I have never known an election where one single issue was before the people, and everything else wiped to one side to the extent it was in the election of 1911. Reciprocity was the issue, and upon that issue the people of western Ontario, at all events, pronounced. The statements that have been made by prominent men in the United States as to what their object was in that reciprocity agreement have been confirmed to the very letter. By whom? By no less a person than the ex-President of the United States, Mr. Taft. Fortunately for us, we know just what the object of the United States Government was when they invited these two innocents to Washington to put it all over them, as they certainly did. I just wish to quote a paragraph from ex-President Taft's letter to Colonel Roosevelt, which ex-President Taft himself made public on April 25, 1912.
I am sure we are all anxious to refresh our memories as to the real object of the then President of the United States. President Taft in this letter said:

The adoption of free trade would rapidly increase the cost of labour in those parts where it is cheaper in Canada, so that the conditions would be the same. It might at first have a tendency to reduce the cost of food products somewhat; it would certainly make the reserve much greater and prevent fluctuations. Meantime the amount of Canadian products we would take would produce a current of business between Western Canada and the United States that would make Canada only an adjunct of the United States.
It would transfer all their important business to Chicago and New York, with their bank credits and everything else, and it would increase greatly the demand of Canada for our manufactures. I see this is an argument against reciprocity made in Canada, and I think it is a good one.
Col. Roosevelt, in his reply to Mr. Taft, dated January 12, 1911, said:
Dear President,-It seems to me that what you propose to do with Canada is admirable from every standpoint.
In the heat of the last presidential contest we got at the real object of the United States in desiring this treaty, which was arranged with representatives of the Government of Canada. The Liberal party afterwards endeavoured to force that treaty upon the people of Canada without giving them a chance to say whether they wanted it or not. Thanks to the determination displayed by the right hon. the present Prime Minister, they did not have a chance to do that. They were forced to the country, and the people have pronounced their verdict on the treaty, and now gentlemen opposite are not sportsmen enough to stand up and take their medicine like men.
I want to make a few references to another matter with regard to the United States market. The hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt)-you have noticed, Mr. Speaker, that he poses as an authority on almost everything that comes up-this afternoon made an attack on the Minister of Finance for his lack of foresight in not anticipating cheaper money in a short time. He says: In my own business in the city of Woodstock we loan money-he is a money-lender, you understand-and we anticipated cheaper money. And he criticised the Minister of Finance for negotiating long loans when possibly he might have	had better success
later on.	The	hon.	member then
posed as a manufacturer, and stated that as a brother manufacturer he told the manufacturers in Woodstock that they were making a great mistake in opposing reciprocity. In the same address he also posed as a farmer-a farmer that grows wheat for the straw. I will not weary
the House with any more quotations from his speech this afternoon, but I wish to refer to a speech that he delivered on the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. He said: The farmers-I know them, I am one of them-do not want free trade or anything of that kind. He is reported in ' Hansard ' as follows:
They are not afraid of the duties being taken off; they are perfectly willing to have them removed. What they ask for is the open market and cheap transportation. What will happen the cheese industry?
Only last week at Watertown, New York, 3,000 boxes of cheese were offered and sold for 121 cents per lb., while right across the line Canadian buyers were paying 131 to 131 cents, and as high as 131 cents per lb., which means $1 to $1.25 per box. That is, Canadian cheese brought 1 cent to 11 cents per lb. more than American cheese. Yet the hon. member asks what would happen to cheese if we had free trade! He also said that we send milk to the big cities in the United States. I admit that, if within easy access to the cities of the United States, you can sell your milk and get a big price for it, but unfortunately every farmer is not so situated. We have millions of dollars invested in the cheese industry in this country, and our cheese has a reputation in the old country that justifies buyers paying from one cent to one and a half cents more for Canadian cheese than for United States cheese. Is not that reputation worth cherishing? I do not think we can afford to lose it, nor do I think, notwithstanding the arguments of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. L. Thomson), that we can afford to let our wheat lose its identity. He says, if we get the price why .should we care about the reputation? But how long should we get the price if we did not have the reputation? Notwithstanding the hundreds of millions of dollars that we have expended on transportation facilities in this country,^ hon. gentlemen opposite are prepared to let all that go and to divert traffic to the United States, thereby helping the industries of that country. Then they come to free agricultural implements, and rail at the iniquity of the prices charged the farmers in western Canada. I remember when for the old style of reaper we used to pay as high as from $200 to $225. To-day for a binder, up-to-date in every respect, the cost of the whole outfit is $140. The policy that has developed those industries

in this country was referred to yesterday by the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil), who spoke as follows:
I want this Government to live up to their so-called National Policy, as it was intended by their great leader Sir John Macdonald. They are not very generous, our friends opposite, they will not believe that we have improved the National Policy to a great extent.
The National Policy that has now been in existence for about 35 years, is the policy that has developed in this country the manufacturing industries that we have here to-day; that has created one of the best markets that we have in the world, and I believe that the Canadian manufacturers of farm implements are not charging the people an exoribant price for their goods.
If hon. gentlemen opposite were consistent with their attitude of last year, they would not be crying for free agricultural implements. When the Naval Bill was before this House, they protested day and night, week after week, against the iniquity of having dreadnoughts built in the old country, notwithstanding the fart that they could be built there for one-third less money than they could be built for in Canada. My hon. friends opposite were great protectionists then. They said that these dreadnoughts must be built in Canada; that the money must be spent in Canada; that nothing else would suit them. To-day they are prepared to let the American manufacturers supply us with agricultural implements. I cannot understand any party committing political suicide as the Liberal party are endeavouring to do. I do not think we should take them seriously; I do not believe they take themselves seriously; I think they are just waiting, Micawber-like, in the hope that something will happen. I believe they would be tickled to death if some great calamity were to overtake the people of Canada, so that they could point to it as a result of the election of the 21st of September, 1911.
My hon. friends opposite seem to be very much afraid of mixed farming. I gee the hon. member for West Kent (Mr. McCoig) smiling. I do not believe he was in earnest in anticipating that this province would be overrun with those wild hogs from western Canada. What has happened? During the contest of 1911, I said that undoubtedly there were some things for which we would receive a higher price in the United States than we would receive here; but that taking it on the whole, we stood to lose by the reciprocity treaty. The time had come 
in the history of this country when protection was of some tangible value to our farmers, and it was not until that time had arrived that there was any disposition on the part of the United States to enter into a reciprocity arrangement. When the old treaty was abrogated by the United States without a moment's warning, after we had developed trade between the two countries, we had to find new channels of trade. While doing that, we had undoubtedly a few years in this country when reciprocity would have been favoured by the Canadian people; tout if that treaty had not been abrogated at that time, I am absolutely sure that Canada would have before this become an adjunct of the United States, and we would not have had the manufacturing industries in this country that we have to-day.
Hon. gentlemen opposite will question whether the United States or Canada is the better market. I will give the figures for
1912	and 1913 on a few items of agricultural products that are sold between the two countries under the present tariff. In 1912, we imported from the United States 19,830 horses and we sold them 4,160. We were told what a great market we had in the United States for our horses, whereas they were coming across the border in spite of a heavy duty and filling the market which we ought to have supplied ourselves. In
1913	16,813 American horses were sent to
Canada and we sold to the United States 1,770. I remember well, when American sheep were being sold in Toronto and other markets during the reciprocity campaign, the Liberals said:	Why, that is a Tory
scheme; they are sending the sheep over here to beat the Grits, and are selling them in Ontario at a loss. What happened in the next two years? In 1912, we brought from the United States, 192,530 sheep and we sold them 10,940; in 1913 we bought from them 229,713 sheep and we sold them 5,340. Of course, these figures will not appeal to a man who is bound to grow wheat whether he does it at a profit or at a loss; but they are facts which the farmers of this country realize, notwithstanding the hot air handed out to them from time to time by my hon. friends opposite.
In 1912, we bought from the United States 1,665,893 lb. of mutton and lamb and we sold them 31,993 lb.; in 1913 we bought from them 4,284,300 lb. and we sold them 34,340 ib. In 1912 we bought from the United States 11,223,961 lb. of bacon and ham and we sold them 82,240 lb.; in 1913 we bougnt from them 13,501,726 lb. and we sold them 154,630 lb.

The hon. member for Huntingdon (Mr. Robb) the other night in dealing with the question of butter, pointed out the splendid market in the United States for our butter and cream. I asked him if he could tell us how much butter had been imported into Canada from the United States, but he could not tell me. He was only giving one side of the ledger. I am giving both sides and you can draw your own conclusions. In 1912 we bought from the United States 929,318 lib. of butter and we sold them 590,480 lb.; in 1913 we bought from them 1,100,431 lb. and we sold them 304,503 lb. In 1912 we bought from New Zealand 2,139,944 lb. of butter and from Great Britain 700,900 lb. of butter.
All this is being sold in Canada; and yet some people are crying out for another market. What the farmer of Canada wants above all to-day is protection, which will shut out the cheap products and the cheap labour of other countries. 'I was delighted in the Agricultural Committee to-day to see the Minister of Inland Revenue present for consideration a Bill providing for the enforcement of the Pure Food law in Canada, in regard to maple products, and a few weeks ago the Minister of Agriculture sent another Bill to that committee, which would prevent the sale of imitations of our butter and other products. I commend the Government for this legislation promoted in the interest of the farmers of Canada.
It is well to take stock of ourselves occasionally to find out where we stand or where we are drifting to. Canada has a heritage in its vast area of fertile lands such as few people possess, the opening up and development of which requires a wise and careful management to avoid unnecessary waste and to secure the best results. If there is one lesson taught by history it is that the permanent greatness of any nation must ultimately depend more upon the character of its country population than upon anything else. It would be a calamity to Canada to have our farms occupied by a lower type or standard of people than now occupy them. It is impossible not to notice the feeling of unrest that has existed among the farming population of the older provinces for a number of years past. Take for instance the province of Ontario, where I am more familiar with conditions than in any other. The census returns for the past two decades point only too clearly to a condition of affairs that should not exist in a province so richly endowed by nature with all the advantages that should inure to prosperity and content. Having been born
and brought up, and having lived most of my life on a Canadian farm, I have watched very closely the attitude of the late Government, and also of the present one, regarding their desire to promote by legislation the interests and welfare of the farmers of Canada. I have noticed the various policies that have been adopted by the right hon. leader of the Opposition, and the party now in opposition. I remember quite well his free trade policy previous to the general election of 1896, and the appeals that were made to the farmers of Canada at that time, which is indicated by the reference to the right hon. gentleman's speech in Winnipeg a short time previous.
I also remember the statements that were made by the same right hon. gentleman before a Toronto audience on February 21, 1906, as reported by the Toronto Globe. These are the statements of the Liberal party, who now advocates for the moment a policy of free food for the benefit of the farmers of Canada, which is apparently endorsed by his party.
I remember, when Sir Richard Cartwright represented the riding I now have the honour to represent, how he went from one end of the constituency to the other railing against the protective tariff, but yet a protective tariff remained in existence during the fifteen years the Liberals were in poweT. I have before me a clipping from a Winnipeg paper which contains a report of the address delivered in that city by the right hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, in 1894, when he said:
When the Liberal party are in power they will at once give a measure of freedom of trade and step by step they will follow it up, and if God spares our lives we shall progress steadily until we have it as full as Great Britain has it. X come before you to-night to preach to you this new gospel of free trade. I denounce to you the policy of protection as bondage, yes bondage, and I refer to it as bondage in the same way as American slavery was bondage. Sir, our policy is freedom of trade such as exists in England, such as is practiced in Great Britan.
That was the Liberal policy in 1894, and apparently, judging from this speech of the right hon. gentleman, he had gone back to his old love. But the Liberals came into power, and strange to say things drifted along practically unchanged as far as the tariff was concerned. In 1904, on October 14, the Liberals of western Ontario gave a banquet to Sir Wilfrid Laurier in Toronto,, and at that banquet there was an address delivered by Mr. T. C. Robinette, one of the Liberal candidates, who said:

There can be no full measure of prosperity in Canada unless we have a tariff permanency. I would oppose with all my might as most dangerous and undesirable a reciprocity treaty with the United States, and, however estimable our neighbours may be as individuals, we have had our experience in dealing with their Government that has left in our memories the impression that it would be unsafe, otherwise, in fact suicidal, to make a trade treaty with a Government that might be abrogated in 24 hours by the caprice of a Government swayed and ruled by popular feeling.
I do not believe that truer words were ever uttered than these words of Mr. Robinette.

He must have changed
his mind because he approved of reciprocity in 1911.
It is not strange for a man on your side of the House to change his mind.

Mr. Robinette, after delivering that speech, was followed by the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who did not denounce the doctrine preached by Mr. Robinette, his candidate; and the only conclusion one could come to from that circumstance was that the right hon. gentleman was heartily in accord with it. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, at that time, was trying to convince the people that the Transcontinental railway from Winnipeg to Moncton would only cost to construct $61,000,000, and that every cent the people of Canada would have to pay on account of the construction of that road, would be somewhere between $13,000,000 and $14,000,000. Two years later, in 1906, Sir Wilfrid Laurier delivered an address in Toronto, and in that manufacturing city, dealing with the tariff, he sang a different song from that which he sang in Winnipeg twelve years before. He said, as reported in the Toronto Globe:
Everybody will agree with me -the business men of Toronto more than anybody-that in a fiscal policy such as we have, where we derive our revenue chiefly from customs duties, it is absolutely essential to the capitalist, to the workingman, to the business man, to the industrialist, that he should know exactly the conditions under which he invests his capital; that he should know that it will be invested under a condition that will not be likely altered.
After referring to the changes that had been made in the tariff by the Conservative party he continued-
But I am proud to say that under our regime the manufacturers always sleep soundly and never fear interference with the tariff. We have made very few changes in the duty.
Here, Sir Wilfrid Laurier was trying iby every means to get the votes of the people [DOT]
of Toronto, and his remarks seem to confirm the statement then made on every platform in the country that while he was preaching his free trade doctrine there was an understanding between the Liberal party and the manufacturers of Canada, that if the Liberals came into power the tariff would not be interfered with. I wish now to refer to an address delivered by the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) in the city of Woodstock on March 4, 1911. That hon. gentleman stated this afternoon that he, as a manufacturer, had told the manufacturers that they were very foolish to oppose the two and one-half per cent reduction in the duty on agricultural implements. That speech of his is reported as follows by the Toronto Globe.:
He could not see that the manufacturers would be touched very much, as few articles manufactured in Canada were affected. He was sure the Bain and Woodstock wagon companies would compete in the world's markets even with 2 J per cent reduction in the tariff. He thought the manufacturers opposed reciprocity because of what might follow, the ' thin end of the wedge ', but he had been assured by Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Mr. Fielding that nothing of the sort would follow. They had gone as far in the farmers' interests as they would.
That statement was apparently confirmed later on, by the right hon. the leader of the Opposition in this House. ' Hansard ' of 1910-11, page 5742, contains this statement by the right hon. gentleman:
The statement made by the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) was quite consistent with our policy, it was nothing new, and he had perfect authority, not only he but every member of the Liberal side, to make that statement.
Mr. Foster:	Did the Prime Minister and
the Minister of Finance authorize the member in question to make that statement?
Sir Wilfrid Laurier:	I have answered that
already. It is perfectly true. The hon. member for North Oxford and every Liberal member had such authority. He was not kept in ignorance of our policy in this matter, and knew it well. He only stated what is our general policy.
Now, what are we to understand? For myself, I do not believe, in the face of the statements that have been made by hon. gentlemen opposite, that they intend to move an amendment for the reduction of any of these duties. I think they have been just jollying along, talking along this line without any definite idea of what they are going to do. Possibly, later on, they will come to some conclusion as to the course they will pursue. I was a little disappointed that the Liberal authority in our province, the Toronto Globe, fell down in its prediction that the hon. junior mem-

her for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) -would move an amendment. I wish also to point out with regard to this agitation, which is taken part in by a number of our friends in western Canada, that Ontario, notwithstanding all the hard things you say about it, contributes very generously to the revenue of this country. In 1912-13 Ontario contributed $44,808,000, or about forty per cent of the total revenue of Canada. That is not a small item. And as to agricultural production, notwithstanding the claims made about the enormous value of the wheat crop of western Canada, the farmers of Ontario are doing a good deal along that line. The fact has already been referred to by other speakers, that the field crops, of Ontario almost equal those of the three western provinces put together. Surely, this is a record to be proud of. And with the policy we have in effect in this country to-day, the movement of the people away from the land, has come to an end so far as the province of Ontario is concerned. If you 'leave the protective tariff which the farmer now enjoys, with very slight alterations, you will find that the movement will be from the city back to the land. For, let me tell you, notwithstanding the splendid country you have in western Canada, the lands of Ontario are cheaper than any in the Dominion of Canada considering their actual value and the comforts and conveniences we enjoy. The movement has already begun, and nothing has been more conducive to that movement than the fact that the prices of farm products have increased.
And now I wish to say a word with respect to this free food fetish of hon. gentlemen opposite and also^ with respect to the commission that is now investigating what is termed the high cost of living.
Mr. A. Iv. MACLEAN: Did I understand the hon. gentleman to say that the high *cost of living is a fetish?

I spoke of the free food fetish. Now, I have here a report published by the United States Senate of a committee that was appointed in 1910 to inquire into this matter. That committee -came to conclusions, some of which I will quote:
Increased cost of production of farm products by reason of higher land values and higher wages.
Increased demand for farm products and food.
Shifting of population from food-producing .to food-consuming occupations and localities.
Immigration to food-consuming localities. Reduced fertility of land resulting in lower average production or in increased expenditures for fertilization.
Increased banking facilities in agricultural localities which enable farmers to hold their crops and market to the best advantage. This results in steadying prices, but also tends to advance prices.
Reduced supply convenient to trasportation facilities of such commodities as timber.
Cold storage plants, which result in preventing extreme fluctuations of prices of certain commodities with the seasons, but by enabling the wholesaler to buy and sell at the best possible advantage, tend to advance prices. Increased cost of distribution.
Industrial combinations.
Organizations of producers or of dealers. Advertising.
Increased money supply.
Overcapitalization.
Higher standard of living.
I have here the evidence taken by that committee. They had reports from United States consuls in many European countries. These reports show that the increased cost of living is not confined to any one country but is general throughout the world:
Germany has long since ceased to be an inexpensive country, popular opinion to the contrary notwithstanding. The subjoined tables show conclusively the steady advance of the cost of living all along the line, an advance which is explained not only by the phenomena which accompany the enormous increase in the world's production of gold, but by profound changes which are taking place, which have already taken place, in the social fabric of the German people. Rapidly accumulated fortunes and increasing national wealth have created new standards and new requirements. Shorter hours of labour, higher wages, old-age and accident insurance, abundant tables, better homes-these are among the contributing causes of the higher cost of living, not merely as respects commodities, but as respects total per capital expenditures.
Then, as to Russia, the following is from the report of Mr. John Grout, Consul at Odessa:
During the past ten years there has been a gradual increase in the cost of almost all articles that enter into living requirements in this consular district and city in particular.
And the consul for the district of Havre, France, Mr. James E. Dunning, reports:
The cost of living in France has considerably increased in the past ten years and is the subject of constant comment and continual complaint on the part of those whose salaries remain unchanged. Moreover, there is every indication that the augmentation will continue, and that ten years hence we shall be paying still more for the necessaries of life than today.
Indeed, the modern Frenchman could very well say:	1 Give us the luxuries of life and
we will dispense with the necessities.'
Wo may say the same thing of Canada. That is one of the reasons why the cost of

living has gone np. And if food products are put on the free list in this country, if you are going to allow the countries which produce with cheaper labour than Canada, countries where other conditions may be more favourable, to send their products in-* to Canada free of duty, if you are going to allow the surplus of other protected countries to be unloaded in Canada, you are going to do something that will injure Canadian agriculture. For if there ever was a country under the sun that ought to be termed an agricultural country it is Canada; and it is a shame and disgrace to the country that we have to import from Australia, New Zealand, South America, the United States or any other country the millions and millions of dollars worth of stuff that is being consumed by the people of our own country.
I have spoken at greater length than I intended to, but this is too serious a question to be treated in a frivolous manner. Tariff changes cannot be considered lightly; we must consider what the effect of any proposed change is going to be in the country that we are a.11 so anxious to see prosper and fulfil the destiny which we believe is in store for it.

Mr. Speaker, it- is not my intention to take up very much of the time of the House, but I feel that it is my duty to say a few words in this Budget debate. As the representative of a constituency in western Canada I propose to deal more particularly with the matter of free wheat and free agricultural implements and I would first like to reply to some of the arguments which have been advanced by the horn, member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) to-night.
The hon. gentleman claims that the members from the West talk about nothing but free wheat, and he advocates a home market. I would like to ask him where he would find a home market for the surplus wheat that was grown in the Canadian West last year? We raised last year 199,821,586 bushels of wheat and exported 95,311,802 bushels. I do not see any reasonableness in his advising the western farmer to feed his No. 1 Manitoba hard wheat to his chickens, hogs and cattle. When settlement in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta was first begun, the main industry was the' growing of wheat, oats and barley

and until Winnipeg attained its present size there was no market for the West except that which was afforded by the incoming settlers. Half the wheat that is raised in the West cannot be consumed in Winnipeg; it cannot be consumed in Ontario, so the people of western Canada will have to export large quantities of wheat as long as they have no home market for it.
I would like to discuss for a moment the benefits to the farmer of the 5 per cent reduction of duties upon binders and mowers. They would save about $7.50 on the two articles. Everybody knows that the farmer buys a mower and a binder only about every ten years; an ordinary binder will last the farmer about that length of time. We admit that he will save $7.50 in that time, but that is a trifle compared with what he would have saved under reciprocity. I would like to show the hon. member for South Oxford and the people of this country what the farmer would gain if he had free wheat. Take the small farmer who sells about 1,000 bushels of wheat in a year. It is only fair to assume that he would gain about 5 cents a bushel on his wheat if he had free access to the American market. Five cents a bushel on 1,000 bushels means $50, which in ten years amounts to a gain of $500 to that farmer on only 1,000 bushels of wheat. That does not take into consideration the benefit he would receive from his oats, barley and flax. If hon. gentlemen want to be fair they will readily See what a benefit the farmers would have by getting free access to 'die American markets for their wheat.
I would like to refer to an assertion made by the hon. member for North Wellington (Mr. W. A. Clarke) during the course of his remarks, as follows:
I feel sure that we as representatives of the eastern portion of the Dominion of Canada can go to our people without any sins to answer for, and tell them that the hon. Minister of Finance has made-if they feel that it is a benefit- greater reductions in the duty on farm implements than the reciprocity agreement would have given them had it been put into effect in 1911.
In all fairness to the hon. member for North Wellington, he surely cannot be sincere when he makes am assertion of that kind. I have here a list of fifteen or sixteen of the implements used by the average fanner in the West, with a statement as to the amount he would have saved had reciprocity been put into effect in 1911. Here are a few of them:
