So that hon. gentlemen will readily see the advantage the farmers would have received under reciprocity, notwithstanding the fact that the hon. member for North Wellington tries to make the
10 p.m. people of this country believe that they will receive greater benefits under the present reduction on binders and mowers than they would have received under the reciprocal trade arrangement proposed in 1911.
The hon. gentleman argues that if we have free wheat our wheat would all go south of the line. He simply makes the assertion, but submits no proof whatever that this would be the case. Our friends on the other side claim that if we had free wheat our railroads would have nothing to do. The western farmer has made a study of this question, and he does not believe any such thing. The western farmer believes that if he gets free wheat, his wheat will still follow the same channel; where we would get the great benefit would be from competition. Every man who wants to be fair knows that in Canada today we have practically no competition in the handling of our grain. Gordon & Ironsides and Pat. Burns have practically controlled the cattle trade of western Canada, and the condition is practically the same with our grain. If reciprocity had gone into effect, we would have opened up the market to the south of us, and the small American buyer and miller would have been allowed to come in and bid on our wheat. The result would have been that the farmers would have got a larger price for their corn, the railways would have reduced freight rates, the men who handle grain would have done so for less money, and the farmer would have been materially benefited.
They say that the Canadian miller can not compete against the American miller; but so far in this debate not a man has offered any proof of that. I for one, as a representative, do not believe in such an argument. I believe the Canadian millers could compete against any millers in the United States or in Great Britain to-day.
Perhaps there is one reason why they could not. There are very few. men in Canada who make so many trips to Europe or all over this country as our Canadian millers. While they are doing that they are not attending to their own business. Perhaps they would be in a better position to compete if they contributed less money to campaign expenses and put their money and energy into their own business. I am satisfied that the millers can compete with those of the United States or Great Britain if they are made to stand on tiieir own feet. The only way to test that is to give us free wheat, and then we_ can see whether they can compete against the Americans. When the western Canada farmers come to this Government and ask for anything, they do not come here as a selfish body of men, as they were represented by the last speaker. They meet the organised farmers of Ontario and discuss their questions with these men from all standpoints before they come to this House with any request. When they asked for free wheat and free machinery, they had taken up this question with the farmers of Ontario, and had obtained the advice and consent of these men before coming here; so that when the hon. gentlemen complain that the farmers of western Canada think only of the West, they are greatly mistaken.
Three or four weeks ago there was quite a discussion on the purchase of stone from the American side. The Minister of Public Works was criticised for buying stone on the American side, and justified himself by saying that in this way he saved for the Dominion $28,000. I would ask the minister how he is going to justify that policy with the western farmer? If he was justified in buying this stone on the American side and saving the Dominion $28,000, how can he justify himself to the western farmer when he denies to him the market to the south, from which he would benefit probably $10,000,000 every year? I cannot understand the force of the argument of hon. gentlemen opposite. They tell us that gentlemen on this side of the House

are divided, that some are free traders, some are protectionists, and some are moderate protectionists. Where do the hon. gentlemen opposite stand to-day compared with the position of hon. members on this side? The provincial Government in Manitoba has asked free wheat and free flour. What position are the 'Conservative members from Manitoba going to be in in the coming elections? Here they are arguing against free wheat but the members in Manitoba are praying for free wheat. The Manitoba Conservative members while in Manitoba are free traders, but while here they are protectionists. Hon. gentlemen from Manitoba sitting on the opposite side, when they were in opposition, were for free trade. I remember reading speeches of hon. gentlemen advocating further reduction on agricultural machinery. We had the members before the House some time ago asking for free trade in agricultural machinery. It would have been more benefit to the farmers than a reduction in tariff would be and hon. gentlemen voted against it, so I fail to see that they were sincere when they were in opposition any more than they are now. Now they talk about protecting the farmer. The trouble with the farmer to-day is that he has too much protection; he is protected from selling his grain in the market to the south or in an open market, and he loses five, six or eight cents a bushel. Then when he comes to buy machinery to cultivate his land with he is forced to pay about fifteen per cent more than he should have to pay. That is the protection the farmer gets. The hon. member for Brantford says that the policy of the Liberal party is, wherever a manufacturer sticks up his 'head to knock it. If that is the policy of the Liberal party I would like to know what is the policy of the Conservative party in connection with the farmer. Every request the farmer makes he is knocked, he is turned down. He has not been granted one thing that he has asked for, and it appears to me that as soon as the farmers began to do well the present Government refused them a market, and raised the cost of their machinery and thus prevented them from making money. If that is not knocking the farmer I do not know what, would be. A great deal has been said about the success of the Liberal party during their fifteen years of administration and whenever you charge the present Government with being responsible for hard times they laugh and sneer.
I would like to go back eight or ten years to the time when the flood of immigration 
into western Canada commenced. Any man with .sense will admit that the flood of immigration into western Canada produced the good times and caused our manufacturers to grow. Every man placed on the land must have 'machinery to work the land and the more machinery purchased by the West the better for the eastern manufacturer.
Hon. gentlemen take great credit for the construction of the Hudson Bay railway and I am sure I am willing to give them all the credit that is coming to them. I trust it will be a great success. It is a very hard road to construct. Most of -the work has to be done by station work. What I request of this Government is to take over the Canadian Northern road from The Pas to Dauphin, build it up to a standard road, and operate it as a Government road. If the Government investigate this matter they will come to the conclusion that The Pas is not the proper starting point for a road, and I am satisfied if they look into the question they will take over the Canadian Northern railway, about three hundred miles in length and establish the terminal point in Dauphin. It is much easier for other roads to get to' the Government road at Dauphin than at The Pas. I ask the Government to consider this with all earnestness and sincerity and I am satisfied if they do they will adopt that policy.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to occupy the time cf the House to any great length, but as a representative of a rural constituency,
I feel it my duty to place my views before Parliament upon the questions that are being discussed in Parliament at the present time. I regret that the tariff question cannot !be considered on its merits, removed altogether from politics. The tariff to some extent has always been made a political football in Canada and I presume that it always will be. It has formed the platform of both political parties for a great many years, and is likely to continue to be the platform on which we shall go to the people in times to come.
I want to congratulate the Minister of Finance upon the splendid Budget speech he delivered this session. He has, I believe, the confidence of the people of Canada, and has behind him in this House the united support of the Conservative representatives, who are proud of him as one of their leaders and as the Finance Minister of Canada. The people of Canada-Conservatives, Independents, and Independent Liberals-look to him with confidence and

believe that he will administer the high duties of his office with satisfaction to this Parliament and to the people of Canada as a whole. He has announced this year a surplus of $36,000,000 over and above expenditure. That is a record of which he may justly feel proud. It is a larger surplus than any Liberal minister has been able to announce to this House in the past. When the Liberal party came into power in 1896 the net debt of Canada was $258,497,000. When they left office in 1911 they had increased the public debt to $342,042,000. That is, they had increased the national debt during their term of office by $83,545,000. Notwithstanding the legacies left by hon. gentlemen opposite in the shape of unpaid expenditures and contracts which had to be carried out, the present Government under the able management of the Minister of Finance have decreased the public debt of Canada by $6,000,000 in the past two years. That is a record of which the Finance Minister may justly feel proud.
When hon. gentlemen opposite were asking the support of the electors of this country in 1896, they stood upon a tariff platform which at that time they called free trade. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, I think, said the goal of his ambition was 'free trade as they have it in England.' When the right hon. gentleman and his party came to office in 1896 you would naturally suppose that they would have carried their pre-election promises, for I am one of those who believe -and I think others will agree with me- that the election promises of public men are sacred, and that every man who seeks the votes of the electors should carry out the promises he makes to the electorate. Although Sir Wilfrid Laurier and his party had promised free trade as they have it in England, they did not carry out that promise when they assumed office. For the fifteen years they were in office they adopted as their platform the policy of the Conservative party. It was practically the old National Policy. In 1894 the Hon. George E. Foster, who was then Minister of Finance, made great reductions in the tariff. I recall that he reduced the tariff on agricultural implements from 35 per cent to 20 per cent, and there were reductions all along the line both upon manufactured goods and upon the necessaries of life. When the Liberal party assumed office they made very few changes. We are reminded occasionally about the British preference; but, giving them credit
for whatever they may have done in the way of tariff reductions, when figured out, all their reductions amount to less than one per cent on the whole; some claim two per cent; but, whether one per cent or two per cent, their tariff reductions on the whole were very little during all the time they held office. Notwithstanding the fact that hon. gentlemen opposite claimed to be free traders and revenue tariff men, they stood upon the platform of the Hon. Mr. Fielding, which, without any question, was a protectionist platform. It is a very fortunate thing that they did not adopt any other platform, for if they had carried out their pre-election promises it would have resulted in ruin and disaster to this country. It is true that just a year or two before they went out of office they reduced the tariff on agricultural implements by two and a half per cent. I was a member of the House at the time, and I remember the applause that greeted Hon. Mr. Fielding when he made the announcement of that reduction. He was applauded by his followers and the Liberal press throughout the country, but when this Government proposed to reduce the duty on agricultural implements by five per cent, hon. gentlemen opposite told us that the farmers were being gold-bricked. If they are being gold-bricked now by a reduction of five per cent they must have been doubly gold-bricked when the reduction was only two and a half per cent. At the time the Liberals reduced the tariff on agricultural implements, they increased the valuation, so that the duty was really higher than before the reduction. At that time the present leader of the Opposition was a great personal friend of Sir Lyman Melvin-Jones. They were very close and intimate, and I think the home of Sir Lyman Melvin-Jones in Toronto was the home of Sir Wilfrid Laurier whenever he visited that city. In order to please his friend, the right hon. gentleman made him a senator. But not only did he do that; While he tried to make it appear that he had given a reduction in the duty on agricultural implements, he had really assisted his friend by increasing the valuation. About the same time, he made Mr. Frost, of Smith's Falls, another agricultural implement manufacturer, a senator. So we see the right hon. gentleman had very close friends in the agricultural implement business at that time.
Do not you go into that business ?

I doubt if a reduction in duties means very much in the way of de-

creased prices to the consumer. I am a firm believer in adequate protection for manufacturers in order to encourage them to locate in Canada, and to build up great manufacturing institutions in this country so that competition will regulate prices. When you lower the duty to such an extent that you close the factories and shut out Canadian competition, you increase prices to consumers in this country. We have instances where a reduction of duty has not done very much good. Some years ago the Government of the day reduced the duty on coal oil, but no one will say that it lowered the price. On the contrary, it put that industry into the hands of the American combine and the people received no benefit. The price of coal oil was raised by that reduction of duty. Take binder twine, another item from which the duty was removed. The farmer is paying more for binder twine to-day than he ever paid before. If protection had been kept on binder twine and Canadian factories encouraged, the competition among those factories would have given the consumer of binder twine the benefit of a lower price than he is paying to-day. The same argument applies to everything in the way of manufactured articles. It is useless, of course, to try to make the free trader believe that this is the case; but the honest opinion of the protectionist is that competition regulates prices and that the public pays less for the goods than if they were manufactured outside the country and imported.
Hon. gentlemen opposite say:	If you
protect these industries., they will form trusts and combines. In my own county, the Hon. Mackenzie King, addressing the electors, told .them about the trusts and combines. What trust or combine was ever incorporated under a Conservative Government? They are all the products of hon. gentlemen opposite, if there are any combines in' Canada. Although my hon. friends opposite talk of trusts and combines when they are out of office, they never did anything during their term of office to interfere with them.
Do you think there are any trusts and combines in Canada?

I do not think there are. Hon. gentlemen opposite say there are, but 1 doubt it.
We have a strange conglomeration of ideas on the tariff among hon. gentlemen opposite. Our good-natured, smiling, and very able friend, the hon. member for

Red Deer (Mr. Clark), is, I believe, an honest free trader at heart, but he is a little unfortunate in his record. He was a member of this House for a good many years supporting the late Government. He stood upon the platform of Mr. Fielding's tariff and during all the years I have been in the House with the hon. gentleman, I cannot at this moment recall his ever attacking that platform or saying that the people of this country were being robbed by the protective tariff. He is, however, a free trader in opposition, like a good many other hon. gentlemen opposite. Not only did the hon. gentleman support Mr. Fielding's tariff, but he sat in this House and supported what I suppose might be termed the most iniquitous form of protection that could be inaugurated, namely, bounties.
My hon. friend must again allow me to correct him. For some reason or other the bounties went out; they disappeared.

I am glad to know the hon. gentleman takes so much credit to himself, because I never knew him to vote against the late Government during all the time

they were in office and all the time he was a member of this House.
Mr. CLARK-I was not going to vote against their removing the bounties against which I protested.
The bounties naturally ran out. The arrangements were made for certain lengths of time, and the bounties expired according to those arrangements.

Disappear is the same as
expire.

The Liberal Government paid out $16,000,000 in bounties to the manufacturers. I have another case where the hon. member for Red Deer was an avowed protectionist. There is no question that he is a good Britisher; that he loves the old flag and the old land; but he was opposed to granting $35,000,000 for three dreadnoughts to be owned by Canada and to be put into the British service. He voted against that proposition; but he was in favour of a Canadian navy, which has been designated a tin-pot navy, and which would cost perhaps $300,000,000 or $400,000,000. He showed his free trade principles then by taking the stand that those ships should be built in Canada, even though they cost 25 to 35 per cent more than if built in the motherland. In that case the hon. member was not a very good free trader, although now I give him the credit of being almost in absolute control of the Liberal party, because he is gradually educating and bringing over his hon. friends one by one to his way of thinking. Perhaps it is because they are in Opposition. The hon. gentleman has a deskmate, a good friend of mine and a very able man, who comes from the neighbouring constituency of Welland (Mr. German). It would be pretty hard for the hon. member for Welland to follow the free trade principles of other hon. gentlemen opposite. He would not follow reciprocity; he left his party upon that occasion, manfully and courageously, and he did a great service to Canada by so doing. He helped in the election throughout tne country, because every one knew that he was a strong Liberal but that he could not stand for reciprocity. If there is any town in Canada that has grown and prospered, it is the town of Welland. Only a few years ago it had a population of about 2,000, and to-day its population is 10,000. Why has that town grown so rapidly? It is because the Government of Canada said 179
to the manufacturers of the United States: If you want to supply the people of Canada with manufactured goods, you must come here and manufacture them in this country. You must employ Canadian capital and Canadian labour in this country, and thus build up our towns and cities. The result was that they came over to Canada and built up the manufacturing town of Welland. The time is not very far distant when the old Welland canal from Port Colbome to St. Catherines will be one great hive of industries, established by American manufacturers who have come to Canada to manufacture goods in this country in order to avoid the duty. Surely that is a better policy to pursue than one that would permit them to manufacture in the United States, employing American people in their factories, and shipping their goods to Canada. If I mistake not, that is the policy of hon. gentlemen opposite, that is where the parties divide, and I am glad to see that division. I shall be glad if the electors of this country have a chance to decide between the free trade policy of hon. gentlemen opposite, and the policy of moderate protection which the Conservatives have advocated and stood for from the days of Sir John Macdonald down to the present. I shall have no fear as to the result. We know what happened the Liberal party in 1878. Prom 1874 to 1878 they tried to carry on the affairs of this country under what they called a revenue tariff, and the electors waited for their opportunity, which came in 1878, to declare very decidedly that the Liberals should govern the country no longer. We know that from 1874 to 1878 there was general depression throughout the country, that men were out of employment, that factories were closed, and that the working people were receiving low wages. And we know also, that when Sir John Macdonald came into power in 1878 and adopted the National Policy, general prosperity followed. I remember that, at that time, Sir Richard Cartwright told the artisans of this country that they must work harder and eat less, and when you compare the Liberal policy of free trade with the Conservative policy of fair protection, that is just what it amounts to at the present day.
In 1896, when Sir Wilfrid Laurier was preaching free trade, and promising free trade to the people of this country, he also had friends among the manufacturers. Mr. Bertram was a candidate of his in Toronto,



and just on the eve of the election Mr. Bertram thought he was going to be defeated, and he wired to Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who replied that the manufacturers were not going to be hurt. The right hon. gentleman was carrying on then, as he and his party are carrying on now, a policy of trying to deceive the farmers of this country by making them believe they will do something for them, which they have not the slightest intention of doing. The ex-Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) spoke in Hamilton last Thursday, and he did not preach then free trade or lower tariff before the manufacturers, but, according to the Hamilton Times, says of his address:
Referring to the tariff Hon. Geo. P. Graham contrasted the Liberal policy of a stable tariff under which Canada had known fifteen years of its most abundant prosperity, with the tariff tinkering of the Tories.
In his speech the hon. gentleman (Mr. Graham) practically gives the assurance to the manufacturers that they will not be disturbed, but at the same time he says there must he free trade in food-stuffs. Not very long ago a delegation of the manufacturers of Ontario who support the Liberal party came here to see some of the leaders of that party, after their famous resolution about free agricultural implements. I do not, of course, know what occurred at the meeting; but I should judge from what ihese gentlemen say on the train when I meet them that they are quite sure that nothing will be done by the Liberals to hurt them. It would seem as if the platform of hon. gentlemen opposite is a platform to get in on, but a platform which they do not intend to carry out should they unfortunately be returned to power.
Although some people seem to think that I am an extreme protectionist, I am not so by any means. I believe in fair and moderate protection.
What is fair and moderate.

I think the present tariff
is a pretty fair and a pretty moderate tariff. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Loggie) himself stood upon that tariff and supported it for fifteen years, during which time he never spoke a word against it.

It is pretty high on
woollens.

The duty on woollens
does not compare with the duty on canned vegetables.
TMr. Lalor. ]

And they say there is a
pretty high duty on lobsters. I do not believe in extreme protection, but I believe in, a moderate protection, and I believe we have a moderate protection now in Canada.

Does the hon. member
believe in adequate protection?

Yes, I thoroughly believe
in adequate protection?

Then, will he explain
why the Government does not give us adequate protection?
I should think the Government is giving us pretty adequate protection.

Will the hon. member
explain why he and his friends voted for a resolution asking for adequate protection when we had practically the same tariff as we have to-day?

I think perhaps there may have been some changes made, tout if/the protection was adequate at that time the resolution fitted into the conditions beautifully; it was only a confirmation of the platform the hon. gentleman for so long supported.

And the Liberal party
opposed our amendment, so that they thought the tariff was inadequate.

A fine spectacle these gentlemen opposite present to the people of Canada to-day. They would lead people to believe that there is no difference of opinion among them, and they are complaining about the platform which they stood for and supported during all the years they were in power. For fifteen years not one of them gave a chirp; they were perfectly satisfied and contented with the Fielding tariff, which they contended was the most beautifully thought-out tariff that ever was put in force. But now, when the Conservatives are in power, these gentlemen think the Fielding tariff is no good, that everything is wrong about it. It makes all the difference in the world where these gentlemen are sitting. In their opinion, they are Heaven-born politicians and statesmen, who were never designed to sit in opposition. When they are in power, they say the country is prosperous and that everything is fine, but the moment they lose patronage and are out of office they think the country is going to the dogs. Just imagine these gentlemen going before

the electors of Canada and talking free trade; these gentlemen who talked free trade before 1896, but who never practised it when they got to power. I do not wish to speak too strongly on the question, but I should think when an appeal is made to the people the Liberals will be the laughingstock of the country. What faith can the people of Canada have in their assertion when they know how, when in office, they failed to carry out their promises they made before they attained power.
One of the policies these gentlemen opposite are now advocating is free food. They felt that they were not getting the vote of the people in the cities and towns; they saw that the workingmen who wanted good wages and continued employment were putting their confidence in the Conservative party, and now, in an attempt to get their votes, they are .talking free food for the workingman and telling him about the high cost of living. What is high in the cost of living to-day in Canada? Sugar is cheaper than ever, tea is as cheap, coffee is as cheap, wearing apparel, I believe is as cheap, and, as a matter of fact, there	is nothing of
any importance that is dearer to-day, except	the products	of	the farm.
Is there any other class of people in this country who deserve protection and good prices better than the farmers? When the farmers are prosperous everybody is prosperous. They are the backbone of the country; they are the people who produce the wealth of the country; and I am only sorry that the farmers are not getting bigger prices for everything they raise. These gentlemen of the Opposition think that by taking the stand on free food they are going to catch the votes of the people of the cities and towns.
And fool the farmers.

to give increased protection to the farmer i of this country. What class of people in Canada are more deserving than the farmers? They deserve all they get and a great deal more. There is no class of people who work harder for their money than do the farmers of this country. When the city man is still in bed and sleeping, the farmer is out working, and when the city man is enjoying his evening at home, the farmer is often out working until late at night. There is no class of people who work harder than they do. Our farmers are prosperous we are told, and they are; they are getting along all right. But they make their money .slowly, and they need everything that any government, whether Liberal or Conservative, can give them.
Now, we have been doing something for the farmers. I remember the night of my election, when we defeated reciprocity, there was great rejoicing in the county of Haldi-mand, and I suppose that rejoicing extended throughout the whole of Canada. The farmers gathered for two nights in my town and we had a continuous celebration. I told the farmers at that time what I hoped the Government would do for them. I said: Now that we have a Conservative Government in power, the farmers who have been neglected for so many years by the late Government will receive something from the Conservative Government that has never been given them by the Liberals. I told them I hoped that one of the first things would be to assist them in building good roads. And we tried to give that to them.
You did not try yery hard.

In Haldimand the county council have spent about $100,000 in the last three years on good roads, and if hon. gentlemen opposite and their friends had allowed that Bill to become law, every farmer there would have one-third of the money in his pocket because of the help the Government would have given him in the building of their roads. It is most important that the farmer should have good roads.
Why did the hon. gentleman's friends defeat the Bill?
That is rather amusing. I think my hon. friend is joking.
No, I am not joking, I am in earnest. Why did your friends destroy the Bill?

The hon. gentleman imagines that his friends are in power. That Bill was introduced in this House, a fair Bill. But hon. gentlemen opposite opposed it and the Grit majority in the Senate killed it, and no one knows it better than the hon. member opposite. I think I can see far enough ahead to see my opponent trying to explain to the farmers why they did it. We have done a little more than that for the farmers. We voted $10,000,000 spread oveT a number of years for agricultural education in this country, which I think, will be a good thing for the farmers. Another thing I told the farmers in Haldimand, was that now that we had a good Government in power we would give them rural mail delivery.

They had that
before.

We were going to give
the farmers pleasant and happy circumstances at home. We were going to deliver their letters and their daily papers to them so that they could read them ever night before they went to bed, and I am pleased to know that the Government have carried out that intention. Hon. gentlemen opposite have said:	Oh, we inaugurated rural
mail delivery. The hon. member for Rou-ville is a pretty good fellow; I must say that when he was Postmaster General he was very obliging and very kind, but we must speak of rural mail as the hon. gentleman inaugurated it. It was a fine system; hon. gentlemen opposite certainly ought to be proud of it. The mail carrier was permitted to deliver mail to the farmers along the old stage routes and every other farmer in the county had to walk from five to ten miles to the post office to get his mail. The system was unpopular because it was unfair and the first thing this Government did when it came into power was to remedy that condition so that every farmer in the province of Ontario at least has his mail delivered at his door. That is one of the greatest things that has been done for the farmers of this country. The hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong), who advocated this boon for the farmers when in opposition, deserves a great deal of credit for the study and attention he gave to that subject. We are doing something for the farmers, and I hope the Government will

continue to do a good deal more for them; they deserve whatever they get.
I am not going to say very much about the question of free wheat, because I do not know so much about the conditions in the West; but I do think that the milling industry, which is a great industry in this country, should be encouraged. I should like to see the wheat of the farmers of Canada manufactured in Canada in Canadian mills. This would help the farmers because they could use the offal for the feeding of their stock and get it perhaps at a lower price than they pay for it to-day. Hon. gentlemen opposite talk a great deal about free wheat, but gentlemen from the AA^est, not members of this House, who have conversed with me in the matter, have expressed the opinion that free wheat would not be as great boon for the West as our friends would make it appear to be. I was talking to a gentleman a few days ago who raised twelve thousand bushels of wheat last year. So far as he was concerned, he did not know that free wheat would be a great benefit to him. He did tell me, however, of one thing that would be an advantage to him-and I quite agree with him on that point-the securing of lower freight rates from the West. Transportation is the important question in the West to-day, but 'hon. gentlemen opposite by their transportation policy and by the building of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway have done away with the possibility of cheaper transportation in this country for many years to come. If members from the West, having in mind the building of the Transcontinental railway, voted as they should vote, they would vote against the Liberal party on any question. I shall not speak of the commission appointed to investigate the construction of the railway, whose report proved beyond all manner of doubt that over $40,000,000 was absolutely wasted through gross mismanagement in the construction of the road. Further, I submit that the construction of that part of the road between Levis and Moncton was a sheer waste of money. In that part of the country it parallels the Intercolonial, a government owned road, and through the building of this line $75,000,000 have .been thrown away. Aside, however, from this waste of money, the thing was a had bargain for Canada; hon. gentlemen entered upon a policy of building a road that will cost so much money chat transportation can never be cheapened in this country-and that is the most unfortunate feature of the whole matter.

If we ground
twice as many barrels of flour as we do today, where would we sell it?

In the British market, I
presume.
How?
The same as we would sell what we are selling now.
The British miller wants to buy wheat.

Wheat and flour both. We would not expect to manufacture all the flour, but we could manufacture a considerable portion of it. I claim that the Grand Trunk Pacific railway was a bad bargain for this country; it has killed cheap transportation for all time to come. The farmers of the West will for generations contribute five cents a bushel towards the bad bargain and the mismanagement of hon. gentlemen opposite in connection with the Transcontinental railway; that is one of the greatest taxes the farmer of the West has o pay.
I have already said that I do not believe there is anything too good for the farmers either of western or of eastern Canada. I would be prepared to support the building of Canadian freight steamers to carry our wheat and our farm products to the British market. This would seem to be the only way of remedying the transportation bungle that was made by hon. gentlemen opposite and the only way of cheapening ocean transportation. I hope the Government will inaugurate a system of cheap ocean transportation in the interests of the farmers as a whole, and particularly in the interests of the farmers of the West.
An hon. gentleman speaking from the other side of the House the other day-I think it was the hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll)-read from a paper, a copy of which I have before me, figures by which he endeavoured to show that flour was selling at Halifax at $6.50 a barrel and in London at $4.18 a barrel. If the hon. gentleman had read from another portion of the very paper from which he was reading he would have seen that his figures are wrong, and that there is not such a large difference in the prices. AVhile I am not a miller, I know something about what it costs to make a barrel of flour. It takes two and one-third bushels of wheat to make 100 pounds of flcur. On a basis of 90 cents a bushel at Fort William, it would cost $2.10 a hundredweight for flour, 10 cents for the bag, and 20

cents for manufacturing, a total of $2.40. Deducting 36 cents for offal and adding 20 cents for freight, we have a total of $2.24, so that a barrel containing 200 pounds of flour would cost, delivered at Montreal, $4.48. The figures given by the hon. gentleman were, therefore, wrong, but he was doing only what hon. gentlemen on the other side are so fond of doing-knocking some industry. All that an industry has to do is pop up its head and the hon. gentleman will knock it as hard as he possibly can. When he was making that assertion he was knocking the milling industry.
I	am interested in an industry which has received some attention on the part of
of hon. gentlemen opposite. I
II	p.m. refer to the canning industry,
of which I think all Canadians have just reason to feel proud. The Dominion canners have, I think, about 60 canning factories in Canada and the independent canning factories have about 50. I want to say this about the Canadian canning industry: Whether the goods are produced by the Dominion or by the independent canners, Canadian canned goods are a credit to Canada. The aim of the industry has been continually to improve the quality of the goods; they have done that, and to-day the canned goods of Canada compare favourably with the canned goods of any other country in the world. Ten years ago, when the Dominion Canners was organized, the canning business in Canada was in a bad condition. The factories were not in good shape and the machinery was not adequate or up-to-date, but to-day the canning factories in Canada, whether they belong to the company of which I happen to be a member or whether they belong to the independent canners, are a credit to the country. You can travel through the United States from end to end but you will not find canning factories that compare with those in Canada to-day. The goods that are done up are pure, free from adulteration and, more than -that, they are the cheapest food that any labouring man can put on his table. The canning business is knocked by hon. gentlemen opposite because they do not know what they are talking about. In my county my opponent for two general elections followed me around with canned goods and canned goods labels and every time he spoke he made votes for m-e because the people knew that my statements about the canning business were absolutely correct. I repeat that they are the cheapest goods a labouring man or anybody can put upon

his table, and the purest and most wholesome. You can to-day buy a three-pound tin of tomatoes for ten cents. You would wonder how the tin could be made for the money. I have seen advertisements for twelve tins for a dollar but that is too cheap, ten -cents is the regular price for th-e-se goods. The manufacturer puts them up, puts -a beautiful label on the tin, boxes two dozen to a case, -and pays freight to the wholesale merchant. The wholesaler, in turn, sells them to the retailer and the retailer sells at a profit to the consumer, and yet they are bought by the consumer three cans for a quarter; but hon. gentlemen opposite are -still pitching in to the canning business and calling it a combine and a merger-.
What about the prices last year?

I am speaking of this year. Last year they were high. There was a failure of the crop in Canada and we even had to import them to supply the demand and pay -the duty and w-e sold them at a loss to fill our orders in Canada because we only packed 40 per -cent of our requirements. Hon. gentlemen opposite, if they were fair, would know that that is the case, but they continue constantly to attack that industry. These attacks are most unwarranted and unfair. The canning business is not managed altogether by Conservaties. On the board of directors of which I am a member, we have Liberals as well as Conservatives and they must feel very sorry indeed to he-ar attacks made on a business that is carried on honestly in the interest of the public. We pay millions of dollars to the farmers and -employ thousands of men and women in the factories and still that business is attacked session after session although there are n-o facts to warrant the attacks made upon it. If it is an industry hon. gentlemen attack that industry. They are so disappointed over the defeat of reciprocity -that they attack everybody for it and especially the manufacturers; if they would only look a little farther they might rope in the farmers and blame them a little. It looks now as if they wanted io get even with -the farmer by giving free food so that -the farmer would suffer -along with the manufacturer. We know that there is a business depression in Canada. Everybody knows that. All you have to do is to be interested in any business, to hold stock in any concern in Canada and you will know that there is -a depression. Canada is not the only country with a business de-

pression. I am interested in manufacturing in the United States as well as in Canada and depression exists over there to a greater extent than here. I know the conditions 'because I am interested on both sides of the line. The depression is great here, but it is greater there. The New York Central road has laid off 25,000 men lately. On the short road from Buffalo to Niagara Falls and Lockport they have actually in the past month taken thirty trains off that short run. That applies to the whole country. The depression that exists there exists here, and I claim that it is not wise, it is not a proper policy, for members of Parliament in a Canadian House of Commons to decry and knock their country. I claim more than that, that the men who are in this House from western Canada, from Alberta and Saskatchewan, have done their provinces more harm in this House this session than all the good they can ever do. Who would ever think of taking up a farm in the West and settling there after reading one of the speeches of hon. gentlemen opposite. They are doing everything they can to stop immigration into that country. They are doing everything they can in this House to stop prosperity and immigration in the very provinces from which they come; and I say to hon. gentlemen opposite that if they would take some of the wealth that they have made out of western lands, which they and their friends got cheaply probably from the Government that was in power, and invest that capital, which they have taken out of the settlers of that country, in the establishing of manufacturing institutions in their province and their own towns, they would do a great deal more for their conutry than they are now doing. I say, in conclusion, that we should not knock our own country; we should try and boost it. I say, do not knock, but boost, and if we will all do that we may bring about the prosperity that should prevail in this great Dominion always; and if we can grow in the future as we have done in the past everybody, including the merchant, the manufacturer, the artisan and the farmer will be prosperous and successful.

Mr. Speaker, it is always a delight to listen to the beautiful unpartisan method in which the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Lalor) presents his case when he speaks before this House. He is enjoyable to that
extent, but I really think that he believes
a great many of his own statements. He referred to what he called the unfulfilled pledges of Sir Wilfrid Laurier prior to 1896, when Sir Wilfrid Laurier was appealing for the suffrages of the people of Canada on what he called then a policy of free trade as it is in England. I might remind the hon. member, although it is a tu quoque argument, that his own leader, prior to 1911, went to the provinces of western Canada promising them that if he were returned to power he would give to them the control of their natural resources. As yet we have heard nothing of that, although this Government has been in power something over two years. This was one of the main planks of the platform of the Conservative party in western Canada. It was used by every speaker in behalf of their campaign. The present Prime Minister also promised to give assistance to a chilled meat industry if he were returned to power. He has been in power since 1911, and we have heard nothing further about that part of his promise.
We have been treated by the hon. member for Haldimand to a statement as to the wonderful prosperity that attended Canada under the National Policy in force from 1878 until 1896, when the late Government came into power. If he had studied statistics he would have discovered that for a number of years prior to 1896 the trade of this country was practically at a standstill, and that it did not increase in any respect until the revision of the tariff in 1897. If he had lived in western Canada, as I have, he would know that that statement applies more forcibly to the West than to the East. He also made the statement that food and clothing were cheaper than they have been for quite a number of years. I am afraid the hon. member has not kept in close touch with the clothing trade in recent years, or he would not have made that statement. Clothing is dearer to-day than it has ever been in the history of Canada. He also mentioned the undesirability of the imports of butter which has been coming into Canada in recent years. To my mind, that is not a very undesirable state of affairs. If a country, essentially agricultural, is importing butter, it must be that the people of Canada, who are agricultural people primarily, do not find butter-making a profitable line of business. If the hon. member's remedy of a high tariff wall against the importation of butter

were carried out, where would the consumer be? That is one of the great troubles of this Government. They appear to absolutely forget the consumer in every piece of legislation which they bring forward. The great bulk of our population is made up of consumers. This Government takes little thought for his protection. We are told of the tremendous disasters which will befall the manufacturer if the protection is taken off his industry, but the consumer can starve to death for all gentlemen opposite care. The consumer apparently does not enter into their consideration at all. We were told by a gentleman who ought to have known better that he would support in this House a tariff on butter, and that such a tariff would be a benefit to this country.
I regret that in the Budget speech of the Minister of Finance the same lack of consideration for the consumer presented _ itself. There was nothing in his speech from beginning to end to give the consumer any hope of redress.
How would you benefit the consumer?
Certainly not by the imposition of a tax.
Go ahead and tell us.
Cannot the hon. member figure it out?
I can, but wrhat about you?

Before the hon. member for Haldimand goes out, I want to say a word about the canning industry. He made the statement that there were sixty factories in the Dominion Canners' Association and fifty independent factories. He also said that the Dominion Canners' Association waB not a combine. I will leave the members of the House to judge whether it is or not. He also gives great credit to the Dominion Canners' Association for the very low price oi canned vegetables this year. I admit that vegetables, and tomatoes especially, aTe cheaper this year than they have been for five or perhaps six or seven years. He might also have said that last year in place of canned tomatoes selling .at three tins for twenty-five cents they were selling at twenty cents a tin, or two for thirty-five *cents. I do not think he would consider tomatoes at that price the cheapest food the workingman can put on his table. As
[Mr. Douglas. 3
regards the question of a combine, he very conveniently omitted the contract he had with the wholesaler as to how he should handle the products of the Dominion Canneries. That was the most beautiful contract I ever had the pleasure of looking at. By it, the wholesaler pledged himself to handle nothing but the goods of the Dominion Canners' Association. At the end of the selling season he was allowed a rebate of ten cents a dozen on his vegetables, and 121 cents a dozen on his fruits. If he bought outside of the sixty factories of the Dominion Canners' Association he was liable to lose his whole commission. That strikes me as a combine, and I will leave the members of the House to judge whether it is or not.
Might I ask the hon. gentleman if he thinks that was too much profit to give to the wholesaler?

I do not think it was too much profit for the wholesaler. The profit in the canning industry is not made by the wholesaler or by the retailer, but by the manufacturer. The poor farmer gets very little for his tomatoes, about twenty-five to twenty-seven cents a bushel. That does not strike me as being a very high price.

I think the hon, member wants to be fair. Let me tell him that ten years ago we paid twenty cents a bushel for tomatoes, and now we are paying thirty cents. Nearly everything we buy is nearly fifty per cent dearer than ton years ago.

I am out three cents.
The point I wish to make is that the price the farmer gets for his raw product has absolutely no influence on the price at which the manufacturer sells to the wholesaler. The hon. member made the statement that the crop last year was a short one, and for that reason tomatoes were worth $1.35 to $1.50 a dozen. On account of a short crop the manufacturers could not fill all their contracts, he said. That is quite true, but although he was unable to fill his contracts, the manufacturer took every possible advantage he could in the way of enhanced prices.
I shall not take up very much more time of the House, but I wish to discuss the effect of the Underwood tariff in connection with the entry of free wheat into the United States. All sorts of opinions have been advanced by different members. The hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Suther-

land) scoffed at the idea that the western farmer should desire a market for his wheat other than along lines east and west. He seemed to think that we could force grain to be hauled a tremendous distance through barren country, and yet be profitable to the farmer growing the grain. The next moment we heard another hon. gentleman say that the great problem in western Canada was not markets, but transportation. How on earth the transportation problem is going to be solved by forcing producers in western Canada to send their grain two or three thousand miles to the eastern seaboard, is beyond my comprehension.
In the investigation into the rates recently held before the Railway Commission, it was found that wheat was being hauled from the prairies of western Canada to the head of the lakes at a lower price than to any other part of the continent of America. Therefore we cannot hope for redress from the Railway Commission as long as conditions of that kind prevail. If we had the market to the south of us, we would have, in the first place, the advantage of competition, which to my mind is the most important one. We would also have the advantage of the short hauls as between the country points and the market at either Winnipeg or Minneapolis, because I have faith enough in the people of Canada, even in the millers of Canada, that when they see that they are really up against such a proposition, they will not allow their American neighbours to monopolize ' the whole trade of western Canada. That argument was used during the reciprocity campaign regarding our cattle and hogs. After the Underwoo'd tariff came into effect in October of last year, it was an absolute boon to the province of Alberta from which I come, inasmuch as we had begun to produce more hogs than we could consume, the first year in our existence when we were able to do so. I have not the figures here to substantiate that statement, but I have an article copied from a Calgary paper, dated March 8, in which the statement is made that in sixty days we shipped from the city of Calgary hogs to the value of $470,000. That is from one city alone in the province of Alberta and these hogs were sold to the city of Seattle, a market of which we never dredmed. By the removal of that duty, which was done by the good grace of our neighbours to the south of us, the farmers benefited to the extent that those hogs, brought at Seattle from- $7.75 to $8.25 per cwt. and the farmers of
Alberta were able to market that tremendous number of hogs within that very short time. I have a paper here from the city of CalgaTy dated April 18, which says that in one day over $60,000 worth of hogs were shipped out of that city for the Seattle market. Calgary has become to-day one of the greatest shipping points in Canada for live animals, and is rivalling Toronto and Winnipeg in that respect.
We are also going into mixed farming, following the advice of the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce, and last year we produced more poultry than we were able to consume. For the first time in the history of Alberta our poultry and eggs were more than sufficient to meet the requirements of that province. If we do not get free access to the American market for our wheat products, we will go more Extensively into mixed farming. We have no home market in Alberta, and where can we sell this produce? We can grow all the hogs required for the Dominion of Canada, but where are we to sell them? We cannot afford to pay the freight from Calgary to Toronto. We have packing industries, and can pack a certain number of hogs; but, unless we get unrestricted markets not only for our wheat but for all our other products, what is to be the result? Ask the eastern manufacturer what is the result of the defeat of reciprocity. If he is honest, he will tell you that it is more stagnant in eastern Canada than it has been for twenty years. When I was in Montreal the other day I had a conversation with a number of wholesale men there, one of whom said to me, ' We have not had such poor business for twenty years as we have to-day.' He did not know that I was in politics. I said,
' Can it by any possibility be true that this stagnation has resulted from the change of Government?' He said, ' I never thought of it that way, but that seems to be the case; the only place where we can sell goods is in the city of Ottawa.' I said, ' How do you account for that?' He said, ' Because Parliament is in session, and so many delegates come to Ottawa who buy goods. That is the only reason I can give for it.' The hon. member who preceded me (Mr. Lalor) is a manufacturer, and a good one. He has one of the best knitting mills not only in Canada but, of its line, in the world; and for the goods he produces I believe he is capable of producing them against any manufacturer not only in Canada and the United States, but in Germany; yet ask that hon. gentleman how business is just now, and he will tell

you that his travellers are not making expenses, that his resident salesmen on the Pacific coast are just marking time. Nevertheless he is one of the gentlemen who did his best to bring about this state of affairs.

Would you advise
foreign competition as a remedy?
I do not just see the connection.
Neither do I.

An allusion was made by the hon. member for Haldimand to an article which appeared in the Montreal Standard in regard to the price of flour at Canadian points and English points. I was one of the gentlemen who received a copy of that paper, and I presume every member received one. I noticed a mistake in the statement, but I thought it was a typographical error. I took the pains to write to the editor of the Standard to find out if his correspondent was correctly informed or not. I received a letter signed by the man who made the statement, and, addressing himself to the editor of the Standard, he says:
Your letter of the 8th instant has been handed to me, with copy of letter addressed to you from Mr. Douglas, M.P., in which that gentleman states the alleged discrimination against Canadian consumer has been very much exaggerated. I beg to state that the undernoted figures prove that 1 underestimated same. Such figures disclose that the difference amounts to $1.70, which proved the figures which I quoted to be a fair average.
I do not know who this gentleman is?
What is his name?

His name is W. Lutton. Taking as his authority the North West Miller he figures out the price at Montreal at $5.70 a barrel, the price in Liverpool at $3.99 per barrel, and the price in London at $3.99 per barrel, for September, October and November of last year. We have heard a great deal during this debate as to the relative benefits of protection and free trade. Hon. gentlemen opposite have evidently taken it for granted that because the Liberal party have advocated the abolition of duties on a number of articles that they are absolute free traders. For my own part, personally, I am always inclined to let them have that opinion, but I do not think they are doing justice to the Liberal party when they make such statements. I do not think the lowering or the abolition of a duty on any specific article means that the party which advocates suoh a policy is absolutely

going in for free trade. If that were true, then the Conservative party is just as much a free trade party as is the Liberal party, because I notice that in the recent revision of the tariff they have taken the duty off a good many articles, although the unfortunate part of it is that the articles on which the duty has been removed are all used by manufacturers, and not by the consuming classes.	[DOT]
It has been claimed by hon. gentlemen opposite during this debate, that the binder twine industry in Canada was ruined by the Liberal party removing the twine duty in 1897. I have some figures here to show that that statement is absolutely incorrect. The hon. member for the Yukon (Mr. Thompson) quoted from a speech made last year by the hon. member for Wentworth (Mr. G. 0. Wilson), the statement that fourteen out of fifteen Canadian twine factories had gone out of business when the duty on binder twine was removed. A gentleman who is thoroughly acquainted with the binder twine industry in this country, informs me that in the days of high tariff on this commodity more factories' were closed by the twine trust in Canada than since the Liberal Government reduced and finally put twine on the free list. He points out that the factories closed by the trust when there was a duty on binder twine were: Brown, of Quebec; Banner-man, of Lachute; the Port Hope mills, the Dovercourt mills in Toronto, the St. John mill in New Brunswick, and one of the' Brantford mills. These mills, as I say, were all closed under the high protective tariff on binder twine. In fact, the industry had got to such a state that the Ontario Government started manufacturing twine in the 'Central Prison, and the Dominion Government followed suit by manufacturing twine in the Kingston Penitentiary, in an endeavour to break the combine of the Canadian Cordage Company. There was one binder twine factory in Brantford which did not go under, and the owners of this factory continued to prosper under the high protective tariff, and they paid dividends amounting to 60 per cent in one year, 90 per cent in another year, and 110 per cent the next year. The result was that a number of people, induced by the enormous profits made by this factory,' resolved to go into the business. You will always find that where an industry appears to be making undue profits, a great many people will rush into it, and so it happened with regard to the manufacture of binder twine

in this instance. A binder twine factory was established in Brandon, and others were established in different parts of the Dominion. However, they were not managed properly, and they all went to the wall, not because of free twine by any means, but because of bad management. Industries of any description, which are not managed on good business principles, are bound to fail, and the statement that these factories went under because the duty on binder twine was removed, is therefore not borne out by the facts.

What is the reply of the hon. gentleman to the claim now made by the grain growers of the West, that the binder twine industry is in the hands of an American trust, and that the price of twine is higher now than it was before the duty was removed?

I think that probably
the statement is absolutely true, that the binder twine industry is in the hands of an American trust to-day, but that is because they corailed the whole raw product. How any tariff can remedy that state of affairs is beyond my comprehension. If it were a manufactured article that was controlled by a trust, I could understand how the removal of the duty would affect it, but when, as in this case, it is a raw product that is controlled, I fail to see how any tariff is going to remedy the evil.
What is your remedy?
There is no remedy so far as I can see.
What is your remedy?

There is-no duty on
binder twine and what more can be done. It might be possible to get at the combine in some other way, but I do not see how tariff-tinkering is going to assist it. If we had a tariff on binder twine I believe the conditions would be just that much worse to the extent of the tariff.
Now, Mr. Speaker, referring to the Budget speech delivered by the Minister of Finance, "I have to say that I regret very much that the hon. gentleman has placed a duty on steel rods. To my mind that is going to be a very serious thing, because I very much fear that the result of the duty on steel rods is going to be to increase to the consumer the price of nails, and all products of steel rods. I was speaking a few days ago to the manager of the nail factory in the city of Calgary, and I asked him:
' What is going to be the effect of this duty on steel rods on your industry'; and he said,
* it is going to put us out of business.' I replied that I feared that it would. He then told me: 'We heard a mention of that very _ thing last year, and I took it upon myself to write to the Minister of Finance, to the Prime Minister, and to the member for Calgary, protesting to the utmost of my power against any such duty; the answer I got from all these gentlemen was that they would not consider it for a moment; that they felt that the effect would be to put the small nail makers out of business, and that they would not do that.' He fold me that the hon. member for Calgary was most emphatic in his statement that under no circumstances would he permit of a duty being imposed on steel rods, as he knew the effect it would have on the industry in Calgary. For that reason I am very sorry that the Minister of Finance was overborne by the arguments advanced by the steel manufacturers, but I hope he has it in his power to protect these small manufacturers in some way should the occasion arise. With the high transportation rates which we have to pay on heavy hardware, such as nails and other commodities which are made out of steel rods, it would be a serious handicap to the people of the country who use nails every day, if the price were now increased.
I do not know, -Sir, that I can add anything further to the debate. The question has been discussed in all its phases, and I have only to regret now that the Minister of Finance in presenting his Budget this year has absolutely ignored the wants of the great masses of the people, the consumers, the farmers, the artisans, and that he has pandered to the wants of the manufacturers. Then, as to the question of putting the East and the West against each other, and as to the charge made by some hon. gentlemen from Ontario that the farmer of the West is merely a wheat miner,
I have to say that these statments are not warranted by the facts. I hope they will grant the wishes of the organized farmers for relief from the restrictions placed upon them to-day in their market.
